disclaimer: Models trained on simulated data. No real telemetry was used and no accuracy claim applies outside this fixture. Not a validated safety score.

runs.name: anomaly_isolation_forest

metrics.note: unsupervised, so no accuracy can be reported

runs.notes: Unsupervised IsolationForest over per-trip driving features, including event rates. It learns which trips sit furthest from the rest of this dataset and flags about one in seven. A flag means unusual for this simulated fleet, not unsafe. There is no ground truth to score it against, so no accuracy is reported.

runs.name: risk_gradient_boosting

metrics.note: cross-validated on 48 simulated trips; not validated on real driving

runs.notes: Gradient boosting estimating the chance a trip contains a Review severity event, from miles, duration, average speed, energy rate and start hour. It is given no event counts and no severities, so it cannot read the answer off its own label. A driver's score is the mean predicted chance across their trips, shown on a 0 to 100 scale. A logistic model was tried first and rejected: in this fixture every non-event feature rises with the driver index while the Review events do not, so the straight line put a driver with no Review events at the top. Gradient boosting can bend, so it separates them. Honest limits: the sample is 48 simulated trips with 16 positives, cross-validated rather than held out once because that is too few to split and believe. Start hour and energy rate are both deterministic functions of which driver drove in this fixture, so the model can identify drivers indirectly. It is not a validated safety score and must not be used to judge a real person.

runs.name: energy_linear
runs.notes: Ordinary least squares predicting kWh per mile from miles, duration, average speed, event rates and start hour, with energy itself held out of the inputs. Fitted on a random 70 percent of the 48 simulated trips and scored on the remaining 30 percent. Honest limits: the energy figures in this simulated fixture are generated by a fixed formula, so a strong fit measures how well the regression recovers that formula, not how well it would predict real consumption from a real car.
